title: BYO corpus record — slack
description: A Slack message. Title is optional (messages have no title). A record with `replies` becomes a thread root; each reply is served via conversations.replies and only the root shows in conversations.history.

content.description: The retrieval payload served verbatim as the body.

channel.description: The channel this document belongs to, named the way Slack names one. The ASCII half of the rule is documented -- `conversations.create` and `conversations.rename` both say "Channel names may only contain lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores, and must be 80 characters or less", refusing the rest as `invalid_name_specials` ("unallowed special characters or upper case characters") or `invalid_name_maxlength`. The other half is not: Slack also holds non-Latin names, which no vendor page states and a live workspace demonstrates -- `conversations.list` there answers with `일반`, `랜덤` and `식사` -- so every character above U+007F is accepted rather than refused for a rule Slack does not enforce. What is refused is what Slack refuses: uppercase, whitespace and ASCII punctuation. The value is served verbatim as a conversation's `name` and `name_normalized`, so a name Slack would refuse is an object the real API cannot return, and a connector that feeds the name back into a call fails against Slack while passing here. The leading `#` is the one to watch: it is display sugar a client puts in front, never part of the name, and stored it also doubles into a `##incidents` topic.

group.description: ACL group owning the channel (default: slug(container)); null means the container owns no group, so nothing is group-scoped to it.

author_name.description: The author's display name, used for their principal entry (this API exposes no owner display name on the document itself).

visibility.description: public = org-wide, group = the container's group, private = the thread's speakers (its author and everyone who replies), who are its members by having posted in it.

readers.description: Explicit reader principals. `user:<email>` / `group:<id>` / `org:<name>` state the type; unprefixed, an address is a user and anything else a group. Overrides visibility — and an EMPTY array means nobody may read the document (admin-only), not everybody.

items.description: One reaction. Slack's own OpenAPI (`objs_reaction`) requires `name`, `users` and `count` together, and types each entry of `users` as a `defs_user_id` matching `^[UW][A-Z0-9]{2,}$` — a value a corpus author cannot know, since it is what `synth.slack_user_id` will make of an address. So the corpus writes the ADDRESS and the router renders the id, the same way `author_email` becomes a message's `user`. `count` is rendered from `users` too: real Slack may send a larger one, since it truncates `users` and says so on `reactions.get`, but Backlot serves every reactor a record names, so that length is the count. Stating it would add a second place to be wrong, so the item is closed and a record that states one, or misspells a key, is refused rather than read and dropped.

users.description: Who reacted, by address. A reaction nobody made is not one Slack returns, so the list may not be empty, and one address twice is one Slack refuses with `already_reacted` (reactions.add), so it may not repeat: the served `count` is this list's LENGTH, and a repeat would render one id while counting two.

reactions.description: Reactions to this message, as `[{name, users: [<address>, …]}]`. `count` is derived from `users` rather than read, so the two can never disagree.

user.description: The file's owner, by address. Slack's own OpenAPI (`objs_file`) leaves `user` untyped, but a live `search.files` call against brekkylab.slack.com (2026-09-21) found every file this workspace serves carries a `defs_user_id`-shaped (`^[UW][A-Z0-9]{2,}$`) one anyway, so it is rendered the same way `edited.user` and `reactions.users` are: the corpus writes the address and the router mints the id.

Who last edited it, by address. Real Slack's `edited.user` is a `defs_user_id` (`^[UW][A-Z0-9]{2,}$`) a corpus author cannot invent, so it is rendered the same way `reactions.users` is: the corpus writes the address and the router mints the id. It is this message's own author: `chat.update` answers anyone else `cant_update_message`, which the importer checks.

ts.description: When it was last edited, as a Slack ts (`defs_ts`: `^\d{10}\.\d{6}$` — every live `ts` this project has read is a quoted string in this shape, never a bare number). Stated rather than derived — an edit time is information the author holds, not a value the response can work out from something else — and checked at import to name a later SECOND than `created`, since the served `ts` takes its six-digit fraction from a hash and a corpus author cannot tell which fractions of the message's own second fall after it.

edited.description: Present if the message was edited. Slack's message event reference: "includes the user ID of the editor and the timestamp for when the edit occurred".

created.description: Creation time (epoch seconds or ISO 8601). Sets the message ts.

items.description: A threaded reply — a full message that inherits the root's channel and ACL. Carries the same fields a root message can (reactions, files, subtype, edited); its time is its own `created` when given, else one second after the message before it.

doc_id.description: Optional stable id for the reply.

created.description: Reply time. Must be after the message before it: a Slack ts is identity as well as clock, so a thread's times are strictly increasing.

participants.description: Who takes part in this conversation. Thread-level, so it belongs on the root message only.
